title: East Timor
capsule: Timor-Leste (República Democrática de Timor-Leste) restored independence on 20 May 2002 after a 24-year Indonesian military occupation that caused an estimated 100,000–180,000 excess deaths from violence, famine, and disease. The territory had been a Portuguese colony for some four centuries before Indonesia invaded in December 1975; the resistance movement FALINTIL, led by figures including Xanana Gusmão and José Ramos-Horta (Nobel Peace Prize 1996), sustained armed opposition throughout the occupation. A UN-supervised referendum in August 1999 produced a 78.5% vote for independence, triggering Indonesian militia violence before an Australian-led INTERFET force restored order; after UNTAET transitional administration (1999–2002), Timor-Leste joined the UN as Southeast Asia's first new sovereign state of the twenty-first century. A major internal security crisis in 2006 required renewed international peacekeeping intervention.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Timor-Leste's internationally recognized territory is clearly bounded and corresponds to former Portuguese Timor plus the Oecusse enclave; the maritime boundary with Australia over Timor Sea oil fields was only resolved by treaty in 2018.
